title: Мечта о кухне  (Dream of the Kitchen)

segments.t: This scene steps back to Max's army days, when he cooked in a military kitchen. He starts by telling us he always knew he'd be a cook, and then the famous owner of Claude Monet, Nagiyev, drops by, tastes his soup and makes him an offer. Here it is in Russian first.
Я всегда знал, что буду поваром.
Даже не президентом. А именно поваром.
Я всегда знал, что буду поваром.
'I always knew I would be a chef.' "Znal" ends in -l because Max is a man. "Budu povarom" is "I will be a cook", and "povarom" has the same "as a" ending as before.
'Not a firefighter and not an astronaut.' "Ne... i ne" is the Russian "neither this nor that". "Pozharnyy" has "pozhar", a fire, inside it, and both jobs end in "-ym" and "-om", the "as a" endings.
Даже не президентом. А именно поваром.
'Not even president. Exactly a chef.' "Dazhe ne" is "not even". "Imenno" means "precisely", and Russians put it right before the thing they want to underline.
'Here he is, our hero!' "Vot" is the pointing word, "here is". "Vot on" is "here he is". "Nash", "our", is what makes the cook sound like one of the family.

'I really liked your solyanka.' "Ponravilas'" is the past of "nravit'sya", the "pleasing" verb from the bar, with "po-" in front to make it "took a liking". It ends in "-as'" because "solyanka", a thick sour soup, is a feminine word, and the soup is what did the pleasing.

'Thank you! I tried very hard.' "Starat'sya" means to try, to make an effort. In the past it ends in -l for a man, "staralsya", and in -la for a woman, so you can tell a lot about the speaker from one letter.

'Well done. Practically a masterpiece out of nothing.' "Molodets" is what you say to someone who did well, and it comes from "molodoy", young. It's used for women too. "Iz nichego" is literally "out of nothing".

'Would you like to work in a good restaurant?' "Khotite" is the formal "you want", right for an owner talking to a young cook he's only just met. "Porabotat'" is "to work for a while": here the "po-" adds "a bit".
'Of course! That is my dream.' "Konechno" is spelled with a "ch" but pronounced "koneshno". Remember that one. "Moya mechta" is "my dream". "Moya" is the feminine "my".

'You are welcome. I will be glad.' "Milosti prosim" is a warm old phrase, literally "we ask for your kindness", and it means "welcome". "Budu rad" is "I will be glad", the future of "to be" plus "rad".

'I am speaking completely seriously.' Nagiyev stacks two adverbs, "sovershenno", completely, and "ser'yozno", seriously. Both end in -o, which is how many Russian adjectives become "-ly" words: "ser'yoznyy", serious, turns into "ser'yozno".
'In which restaurant?' It's the same "v kakom restorane" as in the night-time talk, with "kakom" and "restorane" taking their endings after "v".
'Restaurant Claude Monet in Moscow.' "V Moskve" is "in Moscow", and now the name takes -e after "v". When it meant "of Moscow" it ended in -y.

'Thank you very much! I will definitely come.' "Ogromnoye" means "huge", so "spasibo ogromnoye" is "huge thanks". "Pridu" is the future of "come", with no "will" in front. Now let's listen to the whole conversation again from start to finish.
Я всегда знал, что буду поваром.
Даже не президентом. А именно поваром.
One bowl of soup, and Max has a job offer from a restaurant owner he'd only seen on television. Keep an ear out for "my dream" and "of course", because you'll hear both again.
